videos.description:
Weekly log of what I'm learning while working with humanoid robots in Isaac Sim.

In this episode I cover two days of study (July 6–7), focused on NVIDIA's GR00T foundation model:
- GR00T N1.7 architecture — System 2 (Vision-Language Model) and System 1 (Diffusion Transformer)
- Observation/action format — video, state, and language inputs; real-valued (unnormalized) action outputs
- Action chunking — how GR00T predicts a horizon of future actions at once, and its roots in ACT/ALOHA
- Data format — modality.json and how it maps state/action vectors, with the so101 arm as an example
- GR00T-WholeBodyControl repo — three projects: Decoupled WBC, GEAR-SONIC, and MotionBricks
- Decoupled WBC vs GEAR-SONIC — split upper/lower body control (RL + IK) vs one unified whole-body policy
- MotionBricks — real-time latent generative model for motion synthesis at 15,000 FPS

videos.title: How AI Actually "Thinks": Inside the Engine of a Large Language Model
videos.description:
Ever wondered what happens behind the scenes when you ask an AI a question? It isn't just "searching the internet"—it's a massive, multi-stage mathematical process
. In this whiteboard explainer, we break down the journey of a prompt from the moment you hit "enter" to the final word generated.
What You’ll Learn:
Tokenization: Why the model doesn't see "words," but instead breaks your text into small chunks called tokens.
Semantic Embeddings: How these tokens are mapped into a high-dimensional numerical space where related concepts (like "leader" and "CEO") sit mathematically close to each other.
The Prefill Phase & Self-Attention: How the Transformer architecture processes your entire prompt at once to build a contextual snapshot
. We’ll explain the roles of Queries, Keys, and Values in determining which words matter most in a sentence.
KV Caching (The Model's "Working Memory"): Discover the architectural trick that prevents the AI from recomputing the same information over and over, dramatically speeding up the generation process.
The Decode Phase: Why LLMs are essentially "meaning-aware autocompletes" that generate your answer one token at a time through autoregressive modeling.
Probability & Softmax: A look at how the model uses a final linear layer and softmax operation to turn complex math into a probability distribution, choosing the single most likely next word.
Whether you're an AI researcher or just curious about how GPT, Claude, or Llama work under the hood, this video demystifies the internal mechanics of LLM inference.

videos.title: How Large Language Models Actually Work (Lecture 4)
videos.description:
For three lectures we stayed at the philosophical altitude. This one comes down to ground level: what ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama actually are, mechanically, and why understanding the pipeline matters for every ethical claim anyone makes about them.

A large language model is trained to do one thing: predict what token comes next in a sequence, over and over, billions of times, across enormous datasets scraped and cleaned and weighted by human decisions that are never neutral. I walk through tokenization, where the model doesn't see words but numeric fragments, and the transformer architecture and attention mechanism that let a model figure out what "she" refers to in a sentence. Then I cover the two-stage shaping process that turns a raw text-continuation engine into something that behaves like a helpful assistant: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback.

None of this is magic, and none of it is mind. I bring back Apple's *Illusion of Thinking* result on reasoning collapse. Then I add two newer findings that sharpen the picture: a 2026 Apple paper on refusal neurons, single switches that collapse a model's entire safety alignment when suppressed, and a 2025 Anthropic and Truthful AI paper on subliminal learning, where a model can inherit a trait from training data that never mentions the trait at all.

This is Lecture 4 in a series drawn from my forthcoming book, *Vigilant Hope: Preserving Human Dignity in an Age of Artificial Intelligence* (Ascension Press). Subscribe for Lecture 5, where we follow this pipeline into the public sphere and ask what happens to truth once machines can generate plausible language at industrial scale.

videos.title: HyperRealm: Hyperbolic Vision Language Models for Real-World Hierarchical Multimodal Understanding
videos.description:
This work was honored with the Industry Innovation Award at CVPR 2026.

Real-world multimodal data naturally exhibits hierarchical structure, yet standard VLMs like CLIP align images and text in Euclidean space, which cannot preserve tree-like hierarchies. HyperRealm embeds images and text in a Poincaré ball to encode hierarchical relationships, introducing an adaptive entropy-driven entailment loss. Evaluated on 18 zero-shot classification benchmarks, it shows consistent improvements over Euclidean CLIP baselines.

Paper: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/AI4RWC/papers/Srivastava_HyperRealm_Hyperbolic_Vision_Language_Models_for_Real-World_Hierarchical_Multimodal_Understanding_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf

Kathy Wu holds a Ph.D. in Applied Mathematics from USC. She is currently an Applied Scientist at Amazon within the Global Store organization, leading projects in e-commerce recommendation, multimodal VLMs, and LLM/GenAI applications. Her research has been published at ICCV, CVPR, ICLR, SIGIR, and WACV.

videos.title: WalkGPT: Pixel-Grounded Navigation Guidance for Pedestrians
videos.description:
Pedestrian navigation requires more than generic scene description; users need to understand walkable areas, obstacles, and the distance of surrounding objects. In this talk, I will present WalkGPT, a grounded vision-language model for accessibility-aware pedestrian navigation. WalkGPT connects language reasoning with segmentation masks and object-level distance estimates to generate grounded navigation guidance from pedestrian-view images. I will also introduce PAVE, a 41k-sample benchmark for depth-aware accessibility reasoning in real pedestrian environments. The talk will highlight how grounded multimodal AI can support safer and more interpretable pedestrian assistance.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10703

Rafi Ibn Sultan is a Ph.D. researcher in Computer Science at Wayne State University, working on computer vision, multimodal AI, and vision-language models. His research focuses on grounded and interpretable AI systems for real-world visual reasoning, including pedestrian navigation and medical image segmentation. His recent work includes WalkGPT, accepted at CVPR 2026, and GeoSAM, accepted at ECAI 2025.
